The Union Army. The military force of the Northern states during the American Civil War from eighteen sixty-one to eighteen sixty-five, fighting to preserve the federal union and, after eighteen sixty-three, to end slavery. Though initially ill-prepared and poorly led, the Union Army's superior numbers, industrial capacity, and eventually superior generalship under Ulysses S. Grant and William Tecumseh Sherman proved decisive. By war's end, it had grown from a small professional force into a mass conscript army of over a million men, remaking the conduct of warfare through coordinated campaigns and total war strategies.

The Union Army inherited the regular army structure of the pre-war United States, but many Confederate officers departed to serve the South, leaving the North initially understaffed in command. Early campaigns saw repeated Union defeats and retreats, particularly at First Bull Run in eighteen sixty-one, which shattered Northern illusions of quick victory and forced massive mobilization and reorganization.

The Army of the Potomac, the Union's primary force in the East under commanders like George McClellan, Joseph Hooker, and finally George Meade, struggled against Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia until decisive victory at Gettysburg in eighteen sixty-three. In the Western Theater, Union generals like Ulysses S. Grant, William Tecumseh Sherman, and George Henry Thomas achieved earlier strategic success by controlling the Mississippi River and splitting the Confederacy.

Grant, appointed supreme commander in eighteen sixty-four, coordinated simultaneous offensives across multiple theaters, exploiting the Union's numerical superiority and denying the Confederacy the ability to concentrate forces. Sherman's March to the Sea from eighteen sixty-four to eighteen sixty-five pioneered total war, burning infrastructure, destroying supply lines, and breaking civilian morale, strategies that modernized military practice.

By war's end, the Union Army had suffered approximately three hundred sixty thousand combat deaths and a further two hundred twenty-five thousand from disease, yet replaced casualties with fresh conscripts. The Confederacy could not. Afterward, the Union Army's occupation of the South during the Reconstruction era involved both humanitarian efforts and military enforcement of new civil rights, though these efforts faced fierce white Southern resistance.
